curriculum.title: Lists and Their Values
curriculum.answer:
## Lists group values together

A list keeps several values together as one ordered value. You write comma-separated items between square brackets, so a single variable can hold a whole collection in the order you wrote it. Items often share the same type, such as numbers or strings, but the key idea is grouping. This makes it easy to pass around and print related data together.

```python
squares = [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
print(squares)
```
```text
[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
```

The variable `squares` holds one list value. Inside the brackets, each item keeps its position: `1` first, then `4`, and so on. Printing the variable shows the whole group with brackets and commas.

You can also build a list from variables you already have. The list stores the values those variables hold at that moment, in the order you list them.

```python
a = "Red"
b = "Green"
c = "Blue"
team = [a, b, c]
print(team)
```
```text
['Red', 'Green', 'Blue']
```

Here `a`, `b`, and `c` are defined first, so every name is known. Then `[a, b, c]` looks up each one and groups the three strings into `team`. Order matters: `[c, b, a]` would be a different list.

Common mistakes are leaving out commas, leaving out brackets, or putting quotes around a variable name. `[a b c]` is a syntax error because Python needs commas. `["a", "b", "c"]` runs, but it makes a list of the short text labels, not the values in `a`, `b`, and `c`. Forgetting an item, such as `[a, b]`, runs but gives a shorter list.
